summary: A scatter of part-buried boulders built from five facet-jittered shapes and a pebble ring, parameterised by count, spread and seed, with an instancing handle for the primary boulder.
objective: At three metres the cluster reads as boulders of clearly different mass, then flat facets and a pebble ring, then chipped corners and hue jitter.
example_prompts: Scatter rocks along the stream bank.
I need boulders that are not obviously the same stone three times.
not_for: Any claim about geology, rock type or weathering.
A terrain system: the cluster sits on a ground plane, it does not generate one.

silhouette: eight boulders whose masses differ by more than three to one
every boulder sunk a quarter of its height into the ground plane
no boulder spherical: each shape is jittered before it is placed
medium: flat facets meeting at hard edges across every stone
three separate boulder shapes, so the cluster is not one stone scaled thrice
a ring of fourteen pebbles tying the cluster to the ground
fine: chipped facet corners from welded per-vertex jitter of up to 32 percent
pebbles between 5 and 13 cm across, each with its own shape and attitude
per-instance hue jitter of 6 percent on the boulders and 8 on the pebbles

principles: A stone resting exactly on the ground plane reads as a prop dropped into the scene. Sinking it a quarter of its height is what makes it part of the ground.
Vertex jitter has to be welded: IcosahedronGeometry is non-indexed, so jittering raw vertices tears the faces open.
The tumble is baked into each shape and instances only spin about Y, so every instance bounding box stays exact and the cluster sits where the framing says.
implementation: Call create({ count, seed, spread, rock }); the cluster is centred on the origin with the ground plane at y = 0.
instancing gives { geometry, material, hueJitter } for the primary boulder, normalised to a unit box standing on y = 0, so a placement is a metre scale.
Set a figure or a marker at the perch socket; it is computed from the tallest boulder actually placed, not from the bounding box.
observable_checks: Run scripts/kit-proof.py and count features in close.png: at least two from each detail-ladder band must be visible.
Traversing the group finds at least three instanced fields, each with its own geometry.
Two seeds place and shape the boulders differently at the same count.

known_limits: Authored creative geometry. Nothing here measures a real rock, its geology or its weathering.
The poly budget is the triangle count observed at the default count of eight; a count of twenty costs about 1900 triangles. The budget is per default count.
Boulders sink a quarter of their height, so the group bounding box reaches about 32 cm below y = 0 at default parameters. That is deliberate, not a grounding error.
There is no moss, lichen or contact dirt: the cluster meets the ground with a hard edge unless the host scene adds one.

Palette values are the colours that render: kit-core scatterInstances runs its InstancedMesh on a white-based clone of the material and writes the absolute jittered colour per instance, so an unjittered instance lands on exactly the hex the parameter names.

T2 is the same geometry with runtime procedural surface and vertex occlusion (see knowledge.surface-tier-defaults); it adds no polygons and ships no files, and it reads at stylized-game quality, not photoreal.
creative_affordances: Any parameter may be pushed outside its stated range; the range is the band that was proved, not a limit.
Raise the count and shrink the spread for a cairn, or re-colour to a warm sandstone for a desert scene.

defaults.rationale: A 95 cm spread with a tallest stone near a metre gives a cluster a figure can sit on, which is the scale cue that stops boulders reading as gravel.

T0.note: Bevelled box from the proof log bounds: the cluster spread and the tallest boulder.

T2.note: Every triangle is mapped: both palette colours are stone and all three instanced boulder fields are matched by mean instanceColor within the 0.045 tolerance. Nothing is left flat. Judged on the captures: at the close distance the stone map reads as veined, fractured rock and the vertex occlusion darkens the gaps between boulders; at the 1.1 m detail distance the stone family's course joints read as masonry rather than as a boulder, which is the cost of having no grit or rock family in the six. The occlusion radius is not the 0.45 m the four pilots use: on an object only 1.0 m tall a 0.45 m radius shades most of the body at once, so it is scaled to about 0.3 of the object height (0.3 m). The 0.6 m ground-dirt band is unchanged.

T3.note: No baked glTF ships for this blueprint: phase 9C baked only the two heroes (timber-cottage and watermill).

T4.note: No external asset ships with this skill.
